question: What are the principles of good REST API URI design?
title: REST URI Design Principles
direct_answer: Good REST URIs use nouns not verbs, plural resource names, lowercase with hyphens, and nested hierarchies for relationships. Avoid verbs in URLs — the HTTP method is the verb. Keep URIs predictable and consistent.

interviewer_intent.testing: REST API design maturity and consistency principles
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show awareness of tradeoffs like when to use query params vs path params

sections.title: URI Design Rules
sections.content: REST URIs identify resources — they're addresses, not commands. The HTTP method provides the action. Well-designed URIs are predictable: a developer can guess /users/{id}/orders without reading docs. Inconsistent URIs (sometimes plural, sometimes singular, mixed cases) create friction.

sections.title: URI Design Rules
content: Use nouns: /users not /getUsers
Plural for collections: /users, /orders, /products
Singular for single resources: /users/{id}
Lowercase with hyphens: /user-profiles not /UserProfiles or /user_profiles
Nested for relationships: /users/{id}/orders, /orders/{id}/items
Query params for filtering/sorting/pagination: /users?role=admin&page=0&size=20
Avoid deep nesting: /users/{id}/orders/{id}/items/{id} — prefer /items?orderId={id}
Version in path or header: /api/v1/users

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The key URI design principles: use nouns not verbs — /users not /getUsers, since GET is already the verb. Use plural nouns for collections. Use lowercase with hyphens for multi-word names. Nest resources to show relationships: /users/123/orders for a user's orders. Use query parameters for filtering, sorting, and pagination. I avoid deep nesting beyond two levels — beyond /users/{id}/orders it gets unwieldy. And always version your API, either in the URL like /api/v1 or via headers.

question: How do you version a REST API and what are the tradeoffs?
title: REST API Versioning Strategies
direct_answer: Common approaches: URI versioning (/api/v1/users), request header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json), and query parameter versioning (/users?version=1). URI versioning is simplest and most visible; header versioning is cleaner but harder to test.

interviewer_intent.testing: API lifecycle management awareness — a sign of production experience
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that breaking changes require versioning
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what constitutes a breaking change vs a non-breaking change

sections.title: Why API Versioning Matters
sections.content: APIs evolve. Removing a field, changing a data type, or renaming an endpoint breaks existing clients. Versioning lets you release v2 while keeping v1 running for old clients. Without versioning, any change risks breaking production clients you can't control.

sections.title: Versioning Approaches
content: URI versioning: /api/v1/users — most common, easy to test in browser
Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v1+json — clean URIs, harder to test
Query param: /users?version=1 — easy but mixes versioning with query logic
Breaking changes: removing fields, changing types, renaming endpoints → requires new version
Non-breaking: adding optional fields, adding new endpoints → can add to same version
Deprecation: announce v1 end-of-life, give clients migration time
Spring Boot: separate controller packages per version or use @RequestMapping(path = '/v1')

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: API versioning is essential for evolving APIs without breaking clients. I prefer URI versioning — /api/v1/users — because it's obvious, easy to test in a browser, and works with every HTTP client without configuration. Header versioning is architecturally cleaner but harder to test and document. The key rule: add a new version only for breaking changes. Breaking changes are things like removing a field, changing a field's type, or renaming an endpoint. Adding new optional fields is non-breaking. In Spring Boot, I structure versioned controllers with /v1 and /v2 packages, keeping both running until v1 is deprecated.

question: How do you design REST API pagination?
title: REST API Pagination Design
direct_answer: Use offset-based or cursor-based pagination. Offset pagination uses page and size query params. Cursor pagination uses a cursor token for consistent results in large or frequently changing datasets. Return pagination metadata (total, page, size) in the response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical API design knowledge for handling large datasets
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not returning total count or using OFFSET queries on large tables
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why cursor pagination is better for large datasets and real-time feeds

sections.title: Pagination Approaches
sections.content: Without pagination, GET /users on a million-user database returns everything — crashing clients and servers. Pagination returns data in pages. Offset pagination is simpler but has issues with large offsets and changing data. Cursor pagination is better for infinite scroll and real-time feeds.

sections.title: Implementation Patterns
content: Offset pagination: GET /users?page=2&size=20 → OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20
Response: {data: [...], page: 2, size: 20, total: 1000, totalPages: 50}
Cursor pagination: GET /users?cursor=abc123&size=20 → WHERE id > cursor_value LIMIT 20
Spring Boot: Pageable parameter with @PageableDefault in controller, Page<T> return type
Spring Data: findAll(Pageable pageable) returns Page<T>
Offset pagination problem: OFFSET 1000000 is slow; data shifts as new records added
Cursor pagination: consistent performance regardless of page depth

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: For pagination, I use Spring Data's Pageable which handles everything cleanly. The controller accepts ?page=0&size=20, Spring converts it to a Pageable object, and I pass it to the repository's findAll(pageable) which returns a Page object with data, total count, and page info. For large tables, offset pagination gets slow at high page numbers because the database scans all skipped rows. Cursor-based pagination avoids this by using WHERE id > lastSeenId LIMIT 20 — consistent speed regardless of depth. I'd use cursor pagination for feeds or any dataset over a million records.

question: What is HATEOAS and why don't most APIs implement it?
title: HATEOAS in REST APIs
direct_answer: HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) is a REST constraint where responses include links to related actions. A GET /orders/1 response includes links for cancel, update, and return. Most APIs skip it because the added complexity rarely justifies the benefit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of REST knowledge and ability to evaluate theoretical vs practical tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking all REST APIs must implement HATEOAS
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show awareness of Spring HATEOAS library while explaining why real projects skip it

sections.title: What HATEOAS Looks Like
sections.content: A HATEOAS response for GET /orders/123 might include: { id: 123, status: 'pending', _links: { self: '/orders/123', cancel: '/orders/123/cancel', update: '/orders/123' } }. The client doesn't need to know URLs upfront — the API tells it what's possible based on current state.

sections.title: Why It's Rarely Used
content: Theoretical benefit: client needs no URL knowledge, API self-documents
Reality: clients hardcode URLs anyway for performance; HATEOAS adds response size
Implementation complexity: generating state-dependent links is non-trivial
Spring HATEOAS: spring-boot-starter-hateoas provides RepresentationModel
Netflix, Amazon, GitHub REST APIs: don't use HATEOAS
When HATEOAS helps: public APIs with complex state machines, workflow APIs

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: HATEOAS is theoretically elegant — the API response tells you what actions are possible based on the current resource state. But in practice, almost no major API implements it because the benefits don't justify the complexity. Clients — mobile apps, SPAs — hardcode URLs anyway for simplicity. The API changes state-aware links every request, adding payload size. Spring does have a spring-boot-starter-hateoas if you need it. I'd honestly say: know what HATEOAS is for interviews, but don't expect to implement it in real projects.

question: How do you design API error responses for good developer experience?
title: API Error Response Design
direct_answer: Good API errors include: appropriate HTTP status code, machine-readable error code, human-readable message, and field-level details for validation errors. Follow RFC 9457 Problem Details format or a consistent custom structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: API design maturity and developer empathy
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning only HTTP status code with no body, or returning inconsistent error formats
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show RFC 9457 Problem Details and the importance of not leaking internal details

sections.title: What Makes a Good Error Response
sections.content: A good error response helps the developer fix the problem without guessing. It tells them: what went wrong (status code), why (message), where (field-level details for validation), and potentially how to fix it (documentation link). Never expose stack traces, internal server details, or database column names.

sections.title: Error Response Structure
content: HTTP status code: correct 4xx or 5xx
type: URI identifying error type (RFC 9457)
title: short human-readable summary
detail: specific explanation for this instance
errors: array of field-level errors for validation
timestamp, traceId: for debugging, correlating with server logs
Never include: stack traces, SQL errors, internal class names
Spring Boot 3 ProblemDetail implements RFC 9457 automatically

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Good error responses follow a consistent structure so API consumers can handle them programmatically. I use the RFC 9457 Problem Details format in Spring Boot 3: it includes a type URI, title, detail, and status. For validation errors, I include an errors array with field name, rejected value, and message so the client knows exactly which fields failed and why. Critical rule: never expose internal details in error responses — no stack traces, no SQL error messages, no class names. Log those server-side for debugging. The client gets a clean, safe error message.
